name: Jim Corbett National Park
blurb: Sal forest, the Ramganga and a tiger-dense foothill food web.

tip.title: Dry the Ramganga
tip.text: Fish, and the gharial that eats them, depend on algae in the Ramganga and its reservoir. Set Ramganga and reservoir to -100% and watch algae, mahseer, then gharial.

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Jim Corbett National Park, Bengal tiger, Gharial). Individual species and links have not been checked one by one. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.desc: The dominant tree of the moist deciduous forest that covers most of the reserve. Wikipedia notes sal regenerates poorly here while other trees come up well.

nodes.name: Tall riverside grasses
nodes.desc: Grasslands cover roughly a tenth of the reserve, mostly along the river valleys, and feed the deer and elephants that graze there.
Fruiting trees of the forest edge and riverbanks. Their fruit is food for monkeys, langurs, birds and deer.
Green films on stones in the Ramganga and its reservoir that feed fish.
The most commonly recorded deer near the reserve and a staple prey of its tigers and leopards.
A large forest deer that browses leaves and grazes; adults are a main prey of tigers.
A small grassland deer of the river plains. Wikipedia notes its numbers fell sharply after the Kalagarh dam flooded riverside habitat.
A grazing and browsing giant that can eat up to about 150 kg of plants a day. Tigers sometimes take calves.
A flexible hunter and scavenger, and GloBI records show it feeding on chital and sambar.
A fish-eating crocodilian released into the Ramganga from the late 1970s. A 2015 survey counted 90 animals, many near the reservoir shore.

nodes.name: Indian leopard
nodes.desc: A smaller cat than the tiger that takes deer, langurs and jackals, and sometimes is killed by tigers.

nodes.name: Bengal tiger
nodes.desc: The reserve flagship, hunting chital, sambar, hog deer and langurs; Wikipedia reports 260 tigers counted in 2022.
Drives growth in the dense sal canopy and on the open river grasslands.
Summer monsoon rains feed the rivers and the lush forest growth.

nodes.name: Fungi, termites & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down leaf litter, dung and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.

story: Jim Corbett National Park in Uttarakhand, India was established in 1936 as the country's first national park. It covers 520.8 km² and was the first to come under Project Tiger. About 73% is dense moist deciduous forest.
matters: It harbours 50 mammal species, 580 bird species and 25 reptile species. Growing tourism continues to challenge its ecological balance.
